extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in Russian/Soviet humor and anekdoty
extracted.subtask_description: Describe and classify the features, forms, characters, and cultural mechanisms that make up Russian jokes (anekdoty), including typical archetypes, formats, linguistic devices, taboo vocabulary, and historical/topical variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Russian joke (anekdoty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short fictional stories or dialogs with a punch line; commonly appear in Russian humor and often organized into categories with fixed settings and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article defines 'Russian jokes' (анекдоты / anekdoty) as concise fictional bits resolved by a punch line. They treat ubiquitous topics (sex, politics, spousal relations, mothers-in-law) but also subjects particular to Russian/Soviet culture; many rely on standardised categories and recurring characters. Example: two-liners spoofing Stierlitz voice-overs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes / Named characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of recurring, named stock characters (archetypes) such as Stierlitz, Poruchik Rzhevsky, Rabinovich, Vovochka, Vasily Ivanovich/Chapayev, Sherlock Holmes/Watson, Fantômas, Bogatyrs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each named archetype carries predictable traits and behavior (e.g., Stierlitz: solemn spy voice, deadpan logical leaps; Rzhevsky: vulgar yet accepted in high society; Vovochka: wisecracking child). Jokes rely on audience recognition of the archetype to set up expectations and deliver a punchline (examples throughout article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed settings and category formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are grouped by fixed settings or recurring scenarios (Armenian Radio Q&A, Golden Fish/Genie wishes, animal fables, drunkards, policemen/militsioner, university exam/bilet, medical/mental hospital, cowboys, New Russians/90s), each carrying expected plot mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the category signals the joke's structure: Armenian Radio uses a Q&A with an unexpected discouraging answer; Golden Fish/Genie uses a sequence of wishes where the final wish produces the punchline; exam/bilet jokes revolve around a drawn question and comic evasion. Examples are provided per category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-dependent humor / puns and wordplay (marked (L))
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes depend on Russian-specific linguistic features — puns, homophones, morphology, or taboo words — making them untranslatable or losing effect in other languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that (L) marks jokes whose humor critically depends on intrinsic features of Russian. Examples: name-based puns (mock 'Chinese' names that form obscene Russian phrases), morphological play with mat-derived affixes, and Russian gender/grammar-based jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of taboo vocabulary (mat) as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene Russian vocabulary (mat) is used to heighten emotional impact, create substitutions, or be the punchline itself; Russian's morphology allows many derivations from a few roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mat can enhance a joke's effect or act as the central comedic mechanism. Examples: contrast between expected profanity and an overly polite response as punchline; mock Chinese-syllable puns that resemble obscene Russian words; linguistic explanation that affixation allows a variety of mat-based forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political satire and political jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: A major subcategory; jokes about leaders, the Politburo, state institutions, censorship, surveillance, and historical events (Stalin, Soviet reporting, Chernobyl, Gulag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political context shapes content and targets. Examples include jokes about Politburo funerals, 'Comrade Wolf' reference, and darkly comic takes on Chernobyl and five-year plans. The article emphasizes that jokes reflect era-specific realities (Soviet and post-Soviet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype- and ethnicity-based humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ethnic/regional stock characters and stereotypes (Chukchi, Ukrainians, Georgians, Estonians/Finns, Jews/Odesa, Chinese, Russians themselves) as the center of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes include perceived traits (Chukchi: naive/simple; Ukrainians: rustic/salo; Georgians: theatrical/greedy; Finns/Estonians: taciturn/slow; Jews: self-irony/wit). Humor often imitates accents, speech patterns, or cultural clichés. Examples: Chukcha fridge joke; Odesa Jewish self-deprecating anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-dialogue and two-liner format
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise dialogic jokes (often two lines) where setup and punchline are delivered rapidly, e.g., Stierlitz two-liners and many teacher-child exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formats thrive on brevity, timing, and a quick inversion. Examples: Stierlitz opening/closing lights, Watson/Holmes camping tent punchline, school/teacher Vovochka exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast/paradox juxtaposition (vulgarity in high society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor created by juxtaposing coarse or vulgar behavior/language with refined or aristocratic settings (exemplified by Poruchik Rzhevsky jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradoxical contrast between setting and speech creates comedic shocks and catchphrases (e.g., 'Gusary deneg ne berut!'). Several Rzhevsky examples show vulgar retorts in formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-jokes and repetition/refrain humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that self-reference the joke-telling process or which build humor via repeated expectations and communal chorus responses (e.g., Hussar 'arse' chorus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-jokes expose pattern awareness; repetition can become the joke's punchline (the Hussar ultimate joke where comrades shout 'arse' repeatedly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable-like animal jokes with moral or maxim punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal-character jokes draw on Slavic fable traditions; animals exhibit stereotyped behavior and deliver a maxim-like punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical animals: Wolf, Fox, Hare, Bear, Hedgehog, Lion. Example: Hare and camels story yields the proverb 'try to prove you are not a camel' used to illustrate bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulaic wish-granting sequence with final-twist punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured tripartite exchange (e.g., Golden Fish or Genie) where earlier wishes set expectation and the third wish delivers the ironic or self-defeating punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: trio on an island — American, French, Russian wishes; the Russian's wish subverts expectations (crates of vodka and company). Genie variant often twists a beneficial wish into a hazardous literalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent, prosody, and speech-pattern imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic imitation of specific accents or speech features (lengthened vowels, grammatical errors, uvular R, set phrases) to signal character and elicit laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Estonian/Finnish elongated vowels; Jewish/Odesa accent stretching syllables; mock 'Chinese' names built from syllables that sound obscene in Russian. Accent imitation is a frequent device and part of the joke's recognizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and cultural-literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes reuse lines, characters, and tropes from literature, film, and historical figures (War and Peace characters, Chapayev, Sherlock Holmes TV lines), relying on audience familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizable quotations ('Элементарно, Ватсон!') or well-known cinematic personas provide immediate context so the joke can subvert or parody familiar material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adult orientation — many not for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite some folk or fairy-tale characters, many Russian jokes are explicitly adult, containing sexual content, obscene language, or dark themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that most are not meant for children even when using fairy-tale figures; e.g., Rzhevsky jokes often depend on sexual vulgarities; Vovochka jokes are obscene/risqué.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and era-specific variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes change with historical context — Soviet-era jokes focus on censorship, ideological absurdities, and surveillance; 'vicious 90s' jokes address oligarchs, banditry, and market chaos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article demonstrates how subject matter, tone, and targets shift across eras (examples from Soviet five-year-plan satire to 1990s New Russian jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Black, tragicomic, and taboo-subject humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of dark or grotesque themes (Gulag, Chernobyl, autopsy, dystrophy) to produce satirical or gallows humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chernobyl jokes about mutated outcomes or 'meat from Chernobyl'; Gulag/dystrophy jokes referencing starvation and camp life. The article notes these are used to critique and cope with harsh realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline-driven structure: setup, expectation, twist
rubrics_metrics.description: Core structural principle: a concise setup establishing expectations, followed by a twist that violates those expectations to produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically every example follows this economy: example types include question-and-answer, misdirection (Watson/Holmes tent), and literalization (genie granting wish in a harmful literal way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of catchphrases and stock lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent reliance on stock punchlines or catchphrases that gain independent cultural currency (e.g., 'Gusary deneg ne berut!', 'Гусары, молчать!', 'Элементарно, Ватсон!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catchphrases can be repeated across jokes and become idiomatic expressions; they help quickly set scene or character and can be used as callbacks within other jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of exposition — short setups and efficient context cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes economize on exposition: a few words or a familiar archetype suffice to set up the scene so the punchline can land quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because categories and archetypes are widely known, tellers can rely on audience's prior knowledge (e.g., mention 'Armenian Radio' or 'Vovochka' and proceed immediately to the punchline).
